subject: Communication
title: The Foot-in-the-Door Technique
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Foot-in-the-Door Technique usable.

hook.text: A neighbor asks you to sign a petition. Next week, they ask you to put a billboard in your yard. You agree.

buildup.text: The foot-in-the-door technique starts with a small request to make a larger request feel reasonable.

discovery.text: Freedman and Fraser found people who agreed to a tiny favor were 4x more likely to agree to a big one.

twist.text: It works because we want to be consistent. Once we say yes, saying no feels like contradicting ourselves.

climax.text: Subscription free trials, loyalty programs, and cult recruitment all use this escalation strategy.

punchline.text: The biggest commitments start with the smallest yes.

quiz.question: Why does the foot-in-the-door technique work?
options: We want to be consistent with past behavior

details.summary: The foot-in-the-door technique starts with a small, easy request before escalating to a larger one. Once people comply with a minor ask, they feel committed to consistency and are more likely to agree to bigger demands. Salespeople and charities use this daily.
details.whyItMatters: This technique exploits our need for self-consistency. Small initial commitments snowball into major ones without our awareness.
takeaways: Small initial requests lead to larger compliance later
Consistency bias drives the escalation of commitment
Charities and sales teams use this technique routinely

faq.question: Why does agreeing to a small request increase later compliance?
faq.answer: After saying yes to a small request, people adjust their self-image to include being helpful or supportive of that cause. Refusing a larger follow-up request would create cognitive dissonance with this new self-image, so they comply to stay consistent.

faq.question: What is the opposite of the foot-in-the-door technique?
faq.answer: The door-in-the-face technique starts with an unreasonably large request that gets rejected, then follows with the real, smaller request. The contrast makes the second request seem reasonable, and the requester's concession triggers reciprocity.
